en: The Sūtra on the New Year Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmaruci of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with...
The great assembly of eighty-four thousand bhikṣus was gathered together.
Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others surrounded him from front and behind, listening as the Buddha preached the sūtra.

Seated within the great assembly, the Buddha was like Sumeru, the king of all mountains—alone towering, lofty, and manifest; like the full moon illuminating the host of stars, his majestic radiance alone shone forth.
As if with the radiance of purple-gold, the entire site became golden in color, standing out preeminent and peerless in its majesty.
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with a host of bhikṣus—pure and immeasurable like the sun or a cloud—remained for the full three months until the arrival of the New Year.
The assembly of bhikṣus was silent and serene, with single-minded concentration on the meditative absorption of the Path, free from any distracting thoughts.

Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and prostrated himself before the Buddha’s feet, praising him in verse:
“For what reason has the Honored Buddha come, To travel here for the sake of saving and protecting?”
Having stayed here for three months at the Gabled Hall in the Jeta Grove,
his aspirations being fully realized, now is precisely the time;
the Peerless Guide should proclaim the New Year.
At that time, having heard Ānanda recite these verses in praise, the World-Honored One sat in quiet seclusion to one side and addressed the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:

“Go to the secluded mountain valleys and lofty stone chambers throughout the trichiliocosm, and proclaim my voice everywhere to the assembly of bhikṣus—both those who have newly entered the path and those who have long studied—to all those who have not yet attained awakening, commanding them to come together here at the Jeta Grove.”
"Why is this? It is because the Tathāgata has arrived and intends to establish the new year.

At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana leaped into the air; receiving the holy intent of the Buddha, he let forth a great voice to announce it throughout the trichiliocosm. From within that great resonance, verses were spontaneously manifested, and he spoke this hymn:
“Because you, O virtuous ones, dwell amidst forests, thickets, mountains, and rocks, the time for the New Year has now arrived; may that which your hearts desire be fulfilled.

At that time, the bhikṣus residing throughout the trichiliocosm, having heard this verse, each used their supernormal powers and various skillful means to manifest their bodies, arriving at the Jeta Grove and approaching the Buddha’s presence to observe the New Year. They gathered together with the disciples who had come from various distant lands and regions, all meeting at once in a total assembly of eighty quadrillion (800,000,400,000,000) beings, desiring to observe the New Year.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Go and strike the *gandī*; the time has now arrived.

Having received these instructions, Ānanda immediately rose from his seat and struck the *gandī*. Its sound pervaded the Buddha-field; throughout the great realm of a single Buddha, those in the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animal realm heard the sound of the *gandī*, and by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, all their illnesses, sufferings, and poisons were entirely eliminated, and they all attained peace and security.
At that time, the World-Honored One, with a pure Brahma-voice, addressed the bhikṣus:

"You should all rise and cast the śalākā-voting sticks; facing one another, you must repent and reproach yourselves, apologizing for the various transgressions and unrighteous acts committed against the assembly. May you each exercise patience and harmony, purifying your body, speech, and mind so that no further defilement remains."

Then the bhikṣus, having received the Buddha’s instruction, each rose from their seats and stood before the World-Honored One. Having each offered mutual apologies and completed their repentance for their transgressions, they returned to sit in their original positions.
When the Buddha saw that the assembly had each returned to their seats, he, moved by compassion, rose from his seat, joined his palms, and addressed the bhikṣus:
"O assembly of bhikṣus!
With a harmonious mind, I turn toward you to repent my transgressions.

Why is this? Although my body, speech, and mind may have occasionally strayed or failed, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One—who is the Unsurpassed Honored One—is free from any error, fault, or deficiency; his mind is never negligent, he never loses his wisdom, he has no cravings or attachments, and he does not violate the prohibitions and precepts. Among all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, his venerable virtue surpasses that of the devas, humans, and all beings in the world; he is the eldest in the three realms, and there is no one equal to him.
Furthermore, O bhikṣus!

Whether one has gone forth from various clans to study the Path and practice the dharma of a śramaṇa, their mental dispositions will differ and their resolve will vary; yet within this Buddha-work, there are practices that must be implemented and instructions that must be respectfully followed, and none may be transgressed.

Why is this? If there is a bhikṣu who dwells among the noble assembly and observes the new year (pravāraṇā), yet his bodily conduct is inconsistent and his mental thoughts are discordant, harboring flattery and deceit;
such a bhikṣu should be considered as not receiving the true and correct [teaching], and thus he is not fit for full ordination.
Why is this so? When body, speech, and mind are pure, one is truly and rightly virtuous.

Having received the full precepts of the Buddha, one harbors a heart of reverence and diligence, following the superior, the middling, and the inferior without arrogance or indulgence; possessing a sense of shame and humility, one thus accords with the Dharma and the precepts.

Why is this? Because such a practitioner has no enmity or hatred, harbors no resentment, contemplates the laws of past and present without agitation, establishes the new year, and possesses neither anger nor a mind of self-importance.
Why is this? Because when one's precepts and observances are pure, the establishment of the New Year is most significant.
If one's precepts are not pure, they are no longer disciples of the Buddha; they are like the corpse of a dead man lying upon the ground, abandoned in a cemetery.

In the heavens and the world, the various devas and human beings each brought excellent medicines, divine mantras, and skillful arts, treating him out of compassion; yet they were unable to restore him to life.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!
One who violates the precepts, even if they enter the assembly for various numbers of *varṣā* (rainy-season retreats), cannot save themselves; they have not successfully completed their *varṣā*.

Why is this so? Because such a person violates the precepts and will ultimately return to the state of nature; consequently, they shall receive retribution in the form of the bitter poisons of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, with immeasurable anguish. You must be diligent and cautious regarding this.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this Dharma, he rose from his seat and left the grass mat.

Immediately, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways; lutes and musical instruments sounded of their own accord without being struck; and in the void, the devas rained down various famous incenses and scattered diverse flowers.
When the Buddha preached this "Chapter on the Dharma of Precepts," he addressed the assembly of bhikṣus.

At that time, each of the bhikṣus remained at their respective seats; yet, through the holy intent of the Buddha’s majestic and divine instruction, and by the radiance of his meritorious virtues which pervaded everywhere, they all rose from their places. Their hearts no longer found pleasure in sitting constantly among mountain crags or beneath trees, desiring only this [the practice of the precepts].
Each rose from their seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and spoke these words of their own accord:
“All dharmas are received from the Buddha.

You are the Sage, the very root of the Way, the protector of all; with eyes of compassion, you are most honored and extraordinary. Your holy virtue is unsurpassed, transcending all without peer; majestic and dignified, you proclaim the transformation of the Way.”
At that time, the Tathāgata withdrew from his exalted seat, offered an apology to the assembly of noble ones, and out of compassion for the world, returned to his grass mat.
As soon as the Buddha sat down again, the assembly of noble ones likewise each took their former positions and sat down according to the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the season had arrived and out of compassion for the assembled multitude, performed the *pravāraṇā* three times before the bhikṣus.
When the ceremony was completed, the five bhikṣus rose from their seats, established the new year (*anupravāraṇā*), and having just established the new year.

Ten thousand bhikṣus attained the path to enlightenment; eight thousand bhikṣus became arhats; and eighty-four thousand devas in the void heavens were all inspired and transformed, each conceiving the aspiration for supreme, true, and correct enlightenment as the Buddha preached the Dharma.
Countless classes of sentient beings have been established in the Three Vehicles.

Now, out of compassionate pity, the Buddha has condescended to his supreme dignity to sit among this assembly, delivering them from peril and distress, so that those throughout the ten directions may receive salvation.

At that time, the Nāga kings Nanda and Upananda each left their own abodes and, carrying liquid incense, sandalwood, and various perfumes, went to where the Buddha was. Arriving at the site of the New Year’s assembly, they took refuge in the Buddha and the noble Saṃgha; bowing their heads at his feet, they offered sandalwood and various perfumes to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, and then praised him with this verse:
"Whether dwelling among mountain crags, Sitting beneath the shade of trees, Or wandering upon the great ocean, He harbors neither hunger, nor anger, nor resentment."
"Come and sit to establish the New Year; a billion beings have gathered here.
We offer all these provisions to the Buddha, so that he may open the gate of the Deathless (Amṛta).

At that time, the Dragon King of the Ocean brought red pearls and transformed them into a magnificent pavilion with latticed curtains, four hundred li in breadth and length. It was composed of purple-blue lapis lazuli, which he held aloft in his hands as he traveled through the void. Passing above the dragon palace, from this latticed pavilion, water of eight virtues flowed from a pond to sprinkle and cleanse the ground, making offerings to the Tathāgata and the assembly of bhikṣus.
With canopied pavilions, he made offerings to the Great Sage and the community of bhikṣus;
with pearl necklaces, he scattered them over the Buddha and the assembly of sages.
He then spoke these verses:
“Pure as space, equal and naturally non-existent,
the precepts are most pure, surpassing a wondrous and precious pearl.
Countless multitudes of beings are seated within the great assembly.”
"They all made offerings to those who dwell in peace, as well as to the assembly of śrāvakas.

At that time, bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, and divine kings from the ten directions came together from their respective quarters, manifesting various wondrous and marvelous articles of offering to present to the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus. They prostrated themselves in homage and devotion, inquiring about and receiving the sūtras. Each did so in this same manner, without any difference; they all came to pay their respects and all resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Thereupon, the devas and humans each resolved their minds to make offerings to the World-Honored One and the assembly of noble ones,
praising them in verse: "With hearts already purified, Supreme and inconceivable,
The most venerable elders of the noble assembly Sit within this gathering."
Having departed from all conceptualizations and skillfully removed all defilements, you today receive our offerings; that which you revere is beyond conception.
You constantly transform and guide those in difficulty, [liberating them] from all worldly afflictions.
His precepts and observances are pure, like a precious moon-pearl;
with a mind constantly contemplating the right, he has severed all fetters and resentment.
Today, the Honored One free from defilement gathers the assembly to establish the New Year.
"The mind is difficult to instruct and transform; One must follow its guidance as firmly as Mount Tai.
Eliminating hindrances and constantly practicing the Dharma— This is how the Buddha establishes the New Year.

At that time, after the devas and humans had spoken these verses, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and suddenly vanished. Each returned to their own palace, where they all rejoiced and took delight in the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One manifested a great canopy of cool shade, adorned with interlacing nets of various jewels, which he spread over the assembly of noble ones, and then spoke this verse:
"His precepts are most pure, And his conduct is exceedingly difficult to emulate;
Today, through the joy of giving, He covers all and establishes the new year."
"Offerings are presented to the sons of the Peaceful Abider; their protection of the precepts is exceedingly pure.
Like the peacock cherishing its plumage, the Buddha’s majestic power protects the New Year.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Now, although the Buddha, the World-Honored One, holds but a single assembly each year at the New Year, his rules of practice constitute the protection of the pure path. He disciplines the three matters of body, speech, and mind so they are free from defilement; he upholds the ten wholesome deeds, the four immeasurables, and the six perfections. Having eliminated the six sense-objects, the three poisons, the five hindrances, and the twelve links of dependent origination, he is as pure as the rising sun illuminating the world. His brilliant radiance dispels all darkness, leading beings into the light of the Way. Being supreme, correct, and true, all are brought into harmony; with suffering and joy being non-dual, he thus accords with the Dharma."
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"How joyful it is that the Buddhas appear in the world! How joyful it is that they preach the Dharma!
How joyful it is that the Noble Sangha is in harmony! In harmony, one always attains peace and happiness."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, the assembly of bhikṣus, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and the people of the world were all filled with joy; they paid their respects and departed.
“The Most Honored One was in Śrāvastī, And for the sake of his many disciples he spoke thus:
‘All [of you] are at the Jeta Grove assembly; Now, the *pāṭimokkha* shall be established as a constant practice.’”
Śāriputra joined his palms and addressed the Buddha: "I wish to hear about the *pārivāsika* (probation) for equal vision;
it is now the time for the Truthful One to speak of that which is renowned throughout the three realms. How does a bhikṣu purify himself according to the Dharma?"
“Śāriputra, I spread the grass to subdue the power of Māra beneath the tree;
you all should likewise spread the grass, for that which you have produced shall now be purified.”
Sitting as is fitting for a noble one, this is to be fearless;
having sat down, one delights in desirelessness and dwells in peace within the three realms.
The summer retreat is now completed; such is the disciple of the Buddha.
One should discern for oneself and take pity on those in the world.
Now is the great month of the year; for the sake of the supreme wisdom of awakening, one should be able to sacrifice one's own bodily conduct and see through various sufferings.
For them he preached of all sinful afflictions, so that they might realize countless sufferings;
having thus attained the path, they now perform the *pārivāsika* (probation).
Greed and hatred have been thinned, and fundamental delusion has likewise been removed.
Able to sever the cycle of birth and death, yet not disturbing the root of perception;
having attained the heavens for oneself and also returning to be born among humans—
having thus realized these two paths, one now performs the *pārivāsika* (probationary) rite.
Having already attained the celestial realms, he shall not be born again below;
wherever he is born in heaven, all cravings have been extinguished.
Having attained the supreme dharma of the world, he has realized the noble conduct.
Having already attained the two paths, he now performs the *pārivāsika* ceremony.
All evil afflictions have been exhausted for the sake of attaining liberation;
having already attained the four nectars, this is his fearlessness.
All darkness has been destroyed; all suffering has been overcome.
These two paths of the fourfold supreme way—now is the time for the *pavarana*. When one month has passed, one attains the first knowledge;

when two months have arrived, one attains the second knowledge; in the third month, one attains the third knowledge. Delighting in these three knowledges, now is the time for the *pavarana*. The four wounds have been extracted without remainder; having crossed to the other shore, one dwells in peace and security. The four months have been completed as those who possess nothing; having perfected meritorious virtues, now is the time for the *pavarana*.

He could subdue the dragon kings Nanda and Upananda, shake Mount Sumeru along with the oceans, and cause all the celestial realms he reached to tremble; Maudgalyāyana and his peers now perform the *pravāraṇā*.
“The one who has realized for himself that he is most wise, whose [tendencies toward] all sense-bases are exhausted,
and who is the benefactor of the world— the Buddha himself spoke these words:
‘He always wanders alone among the trees, yet he is like a leader of a herd.’”
He was once the most eminent Pratyekabuddha, and now he is Pāṭali.
In these three places he no longer clings; his mind is pure among the assembly, his three supernormal powers are firmly established, and he has rid himself of arrogance.
Free from desire within the three realms, With a mind neither agitated nor stilled,
as stable as Mount Sumeru, I now perform the *pārivāsika* (probation).
Having already completed the four [days] on the right, The four paths are now firmly established.
The Buddha declared this worthy one to be foremost among the assembly for increasing virtue.
His offerings and gifts bring the greatest peace; in the end, none can ever destroy them.
Having attained the wisdom that gathers the assembly, the Buddha now performs the *pāṭimokkha* (Prātimokṣa) ceremony.
Having fully perfected the observance of precepts, one cannot be shaken by any power;
with the Dharma as food and clothing, one always delights in the mountain retreats.
This is called firm practice, complete and free from all blemish.
The ground of the pure practitioner is now the *pāṭimokkha*.
Upholding the precepts and severing all evils, the multitude join their palms to receive the Dharma;
as the destination for all, all Māras are thereby subdued.
The devas always favor those who are good; they praise those who are fully endowed with the precepts.
No longer beholding the various māras, they now perform the *pavarana*.
Thus spoke the Buddha in the *Navasamvatsara Sūtra*.
